title: Finite projective modules over a ring fibre product
statement: Let $A\to F$ and $B\to F$ be homomorphisms of commutative rings, with $A\to F$ surjective, and let $R=A\times_F B=\{(a,b)\in A\times B:a|_F=b|_F\}$, with coordinatewise ring operations. A finite projective module means a finitely generated module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] which is projective [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. Tensor products are those of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The functor sending a finite projective $R$-module $P$ to $(A\otimes_R P,B\otimes_R P,\mathrm{can})$ is an equivalence with the category of triples $(M,N,\alpha)$, where $M$ is finite projective over $A$, $N$ is finite projective over $B$, and $\alpha:F\otimes_A M\xrightarrow{\sim}F\otimes_B N$ is $F$-linear. Morphisms are pairs of module homomorphisms commuting with $\alpha$. A quasi-inverse sends a triple to the $R$-module $K=\{(m,n)\in M\oplus N:\alpha(1\otimes m)=1\otimes n\}$. Its counit maps $A\otimes_R K\to M$ and $B\otimes_R K\to N$ are the scalar extensions of the two projections, and its unit sends $p$ to $(1\otimes p,1\otimes p)$; all these maps are isomorphisms.

source.place: Tag 0D2J (lemma-finitely-presented-module-over-fibre-product), with the explicit adjunction, unit and counit of Tag 07RU (lemma-module-over-fibre-product), in Situation 08KH (situation-module-over-fibre-product).

proof.text: Write $T(P)=(A\otimes_RP,B\otimes_RP,\mathrm{can})$ and $G(M,N,\alpha)=K$. Tensor balancing defines $T$ on maps, and $G$ sends a compatible pair $(u,v)$ to $(m,n)\mapsto(u(m),v(n))$. For finite projective $P$, choose generators, giving a surjection $q:R^n\to P$, and split it by projectivity [def-weil-pbc-projective-module], obtaining $s:P\to R^n$ with $qs=1$. Tensoring preserves this identity [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Thus $A\otimes_RP$ is a retract of $A^n$, generated by the images of its basis, and projective: a map from the retract lifts along a surjection by lifting its composite with the retraction from $A^n$ on each basis vector and then restricting to the section. The same argument holds over $B$. Therefore $T$ takes finite projective modules to the stated triples.

source.place: Tag 0D2J, functor restricted to finite projectives; Algebra Tag 00NX (2) implies (3), explicit splitting and scalar extension

proof.text: Put $I=\ker(A\to F)$. The quotient identification $F\otimes_A M\cong M/IM$ is [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-over-quotient-ring]. Identify the matching condition with the one in [lem-sfb-patched-module-base-change], taking its source ring $A^{\prime}=A$, its $A=F$, and its gluing map $N\otimes_BF\to M/IM$ to be $\alpha^{-1}$ (with tensor factors interchanged). That node gives precisely the projection-induced isomorphisms $A\otimes_RK\cong M$ and $B\otimes_RK\cong N$, natural in all compatible module maps. Their comparison over $F$ is $\alpha$, since on $1\otimes(m,n)$ it is the defining equation of $K$. In particular they constitute a natural counit $TG\cong1$ on triples.

source.place: Tag 07RU (lemma-module-over-fibre-product), final assertion; use the inverse gluing isomorphism to match the ordering

proof.text: For a triple with finite projective components, [lem-sfb-finite-module-fibre-product-patching] shows that $K$ is finite over $R$. Both components are flat by [lem-weil-pbc-projective-module-flat], so [lem-sfb-flat-module-fibre-product-patching] makes $K$ flat over $R$. Choose a surjection $q:R^n\to K$ from finitely many generators. Let $H=\ker q$, and write $q_A:A^n\to M$, $q_B:B^n\to N$ for its base changes followed by the counit maps of step 2. They are surjective: each counit is an isomorphism, and every tensor of an element of $K$ can be expanded using its chosen generators. Set $H_A=\ker q_A$ and $H_B=\ker q_B$.

source.place: Tag 0D2J, first paragraph and choice of a finite free surjection

proof.text: Projectivity of $M$ and $N$ splits $q_A$ and $q_B$ [def-weil-pbc-projective-module]. Thus $H_A$ is the image of $1-s_Aq_A$ on $A^n$, generated by the finitely many $(1-s_Aq_A)e_i$, and similarly $H_B$ is finite. A splitting identifies $A^n=H_A\oplus M$; applying $F\otimes_A-$ gives $F^n=(F\otimes_AH_A)\oplus(F\otimes_AM)$ with $F\otimes_Aq_A$ the projection. These assertions follow on pure tensors from the inverse maps $(h,m)\mapsto h+s_A(m)$ and $x\mapsto(x-s_Aq_Ax,q_Ax)$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The analogous decomposition over $B$ identifies both base-changed kernels with $H_F=\ker(F^n\to F\otimes_BN)$, using $\alpha$ on the $A$ side. The two maps $F^n\to F\otimes_BN$ agree because each generator $q(e_i)\in K$ is a matching pair. Hence $H_A,H_B$ have a specified matching isomorphism over $F$.

source.place: Tag 0D2J, finiteness and base-change identification of the two relation kernels; projective splitting replaces the cited flat-Tor lemma

proof.text: The coordinate map $R^n\to A^n\times_{F^n}B^n$ is an isomorphism: a compatible pair of vectors gives, in each coordinate, an element of $R$. Under it, $H$ identifies with $H_A\times_{H_F}H_B$. Indeed $q(x)=0$ if and only if both its coordinates in $M\oplus N$ vanish; compatibility of vectors in $F^n$ is equivalent to compatibility in the submodule $H_F$. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-module-fibre-product-patching] to $H_A,H_B$ and their matching isomorphism from step 4. It gives finite generation of $H$. Choose generators of $H$ to obtain $R^m\to R^n\to K\to0$ with finite $m,n$. Thus $K$ is finitely presented and flat, and [lem-weil-pbc-finitely-presented-flat-module-projective] makes it finite projective. Consequently $G$ also restricts to the required categories.

source.place: Tag 0D2J, displayed kernel isomorphism and final finite-presentation argument

proof.text: Define $\eta_P:P\to GT(P)$ by $p\mapsto(1\otimes p,1\otimes p)$. For a linear map $f$, both $GT(f)\eta_P$ and $\eta_Qf$ have coordinates $1\otimes f(p)$, so $\eta$ is natural. For $P=R^n$, it is the coordinatewise isomorphism $R^n\cong A^n\times_{F^n}B^n$. For general finite projective $P$, take $q,s$ from step 1. Its inverse is $q\eta_{R^n}^{-1}GT(s)$. Naturality gives its composite with $\eta_P$ equal to $qs=1$; in the other order use $\eta_Pq=GT(q)\eta_{R^n}$ and $GT(q)GT(s)=1$. Together with the natural counit of step 2 this proves the equivalence with the stated quasi-inverse. On a pure tensor $a\otimes p$, the composite $T(\eta_P)$ then the counit is $a\otimes p$; on $(m,n)\in K$, the composite $\eta_K$ then $G$ of the counit is $(m,n)$. Hence these are the specified unit and counit, with both triangle identities.
